key_terms.meaning: Adding a tiny controlled amount of a pentavalent (donor) or trivalent (acceptor) impurity to pure silicon so it becomes n-type or p-type; typical doping is about 1 impurity atom per 10⁶ silicon atoms.
The thin zone at a PN junction where mobile carriers have diffused away, leaving fixed ionised atoms and an electric field that opposes further diffusion.
The forward voltage at which diode current starts rising sharply; about 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium.
The very small leakage current (nanoamps to microamps) that flows through a reverse-biased diode due to thermally generated minority carriers; roughly doubles for every 10 °C rise.
Reverse conduction in a heavily doped junction where the strong field pulls electrons straight out of covalent bonds at a well-defined voltage.
Zener voltage: the reverse voltage at which the Zener diode conducts heavily and across which it then holds almost a constant value, e.g. 6.2 V.
Zener impedance: the small dynamic resistance ΔVz/ΔIz of a Zener in breakdown; smaller Zz gives better regulation.
A three-terminal fixed positive voltage regulator IC family; xx is the output voltage, so 7805 gives +5 V and 7812 gives +12 V, with 79xx giving the negative versions.
The minimum input-to-output voltage difference a linear regulator needs to stay in regulation; about 2 V for ordinary 78xx types.
β = IC/IB in the active region, typically 50 to 300; also written hFE.
The BJT operating zone where the emitter-base junction is forward biased and the collector-base junction is reverse biased, so IC ≈ βIB.
The gate-source voltage (negative for an n-channel JFET) at which the channel is fully closed and drain current falls to nearly zero.
gm = ΔID/ΔVGS at constant VDS, measured in siemens (A/V); it tells how strongly gate voltage controls drain current.
The gate-source voltage at which an enhancement MOSFET just begins to form a conducting channel; below VT the drain current is essentially zero.
In an inverting op-amp circuit with negative feedback, the inverting input sits at almost 0 V (same as the grounded non-inverting input) without being physically grounded.
The two op-amp input terminals sit at almost the same voltage because of negative feedback and very high open-loop gain, though no wire joins them.
An op-amp circuit with a capacitor in the feedback path whose output is proportional to the time integral of the input voltage.
An op-amp used without feedback that swings its output to one supply rail or the other depending on which input is at the higher voltage.
The 2/3 VCC level on the threshold pin that resets the 555 output low; set by the upper comparator inside the IC.
The 1/3 VCC level on the trigger pin that sets the 555 output high; set by the lower comparator inside the IC.

takeaways: A PN junction conducts easily above about 0.7 V forward and blocks almost completely in reverse, and that single property gives rectifiers, clippers and protection diodes.

A reverse-biased Zener holds nearly constant voltage while its current changes, so it can act as a simple shunt regulator, and an IC such as the 7805 does the same job with better regulation and current limit.
In a BJT the base current controls the collector current (IC = βIB), which makes it a current-controlled current source and the standard small-signal amplifier.
In a JFET or MOSFET the gate voltage controls the channel width, so drain current is voltage-controlled and the gate draws almost no current, which suits digital and low-power design.
Negative feedback plus two resistors and two golden rules (no input current, inputs at the same voltage) turn an op-amp into precise amplifiers, adders, subtractors and integrators.
An op-amp without feedback becomes a comparator, switching its output between the supply rails to indicate which input is larger.
One 555 timer chip, one resistor and one capacitor set a delay or a square-wave frequency, which is why the 555 appears in timers, flashers and pulse generators.
Choosing a device is a design decision: Zener for cheap low-current regulation, 78xx for simple fixed rails, BJT for current drive, MOSFET for high-speed switching, op-amp for signal mathematics.
bank_note: Long answers here are graded on labelled diagrams plus working: junction biasing with the depletion region drawn, Zener regulator with the Iz(min) and Iz(max) check, BJT and FET characteristics with regions marked, and op-amp circuits derived from the two golden rules.

bank.q: Explain how doping produces p-type and n-type silicon, then describe the PN junction under no bias, forward bias and reverse bias, including the shape of the V-I characteristic.
outline: Donor (pentavalent) impurities give free electrons, acceptor (trivalent) impurities give holes
At the junction, diffusion leaves a depletion region with fixed ionised atoms and a barrier potential of about 0.7 V for silicon
Forward bias narrows the depletion region; current is tiny until the knee, then rises almost exponentially
Reverse bias widens the region; only small reverse saturation current flows until breakdown
Label the knee voltage, reverse saturation current and breakdown voltage on the sketch

bank.q: With a circuit diagram, explain how a reverse-biased Zener diode with a series resistor holds the load voltage steady, and state the conditions on Iz(min) and Iz(max).
outline: Zener is always used reverse biased, operating in the breakdown region
Series resistor Rs drops the difference between Vin and Vz
Current splits between Zener and load: Is = Iz + IL
Iz must exceed Iz(min) at minimum Vin and full load, and stay below Iz(max) at maximum Vin and no load
Output stays near Vz because the V-I curve in breakdown is almost vertical

bank.q: Describe the construction and working of an NPN bipolar junction transistor in the active region, and define α and β with the relation between them.
outline: Three regions: heavily doped emitter, thin lightly doped base, large collector
Two junctions: emitter-base forward biased, collector-base reverse biased
Electrons injected from emitter, most cross the thin base, few recombine to give base current
IC = βIB, IE = IC + IB, α = IC/IE, β = α/(1 − α)
Sketch the current directions and mark that the base current is the control current

bank.q: Compare the construction, operation and characteristics of a JFET and an enhancement MOSFET, defining pinch-off voltage and threshold voltage.
outline: JFET: a diffused channel between gate and source/drain, gate junction always reverse biased, gate current almost zero
MOSFET: a metal-oxide-semiconductor gate insulated from the channel by a thin oxide layer
JFET is depletion mode (channel exists at VGS = 0 and is closed by VP); enhancement MOSFET needs VGS greater than VT to form a channel
Transfer characteristic ID against VGS with the ohmic and saturation regions marked
Very high input resistance for both, MOSFET highest

bank.q: State the properties of an ideal op-amp and explain the two golden rules, virtual ground and virtual short, with one circuit example.
outline: Infinite open-loop gain, infinite input impedance, zero output impedance, infinite bandwidth, zero offset
Golden rule 1: no current flows into either input
Golden rule 2: with negative feedback the two inputs sit at almost the same voltage (virtual short)
In the inverting amplifier the inverting input is a virtual ground because the non-inverting input is grounded
Both rules hold only while the op-amp is inside its linear output range

bank.q: Draw the block diagram of a 555 timer and explain its use as a monostable delay and as an astable square-wave generator.
outline: Blocks: two comparators, R-S flip-flop, discharge transistor, resistive divider of 5 kΩ, output driver
Threshold pin compares with 2/3 VCC, trigger pin with 1/3 VCC
Monostable: trigger sets output high, capacitor charges through R until 2/3 VCC, delay T = 1.1 RC
Astable: capacitor charges through RA + RB and discharges through RB, giving two levels 1/3 and 2/3 VCC
Duty cycle and frequency formulas, and a labelled capacitor waveform

bank.q: A silicon diode in series with a 1 kΩ resistor is connected to a 6 V supply. Assuming a 0.7 V diode drop, find the forward current and the power lost in the diode. Then reverse the diode and state the new current, taking reverse saturation current as 1 μA.
outline: Forward: V across resistor = 6 − 0.7 = 5.3 V
Diode power = 0.7 × 5.3 mA ≈ 3.7 mW
Reverse: diode blocks, current ≈ 1 μA, almost the whole 6 V appears across the diode
State that this asymmetry is what makes rectification possible

bank.q: A 6 V Zener regulator feeds a load that draws 0 to 50 mA from an input that varies between 10 V and 14 V. Choose the series resistor and a Zener rating, using Iz(min) = 5 mA and Iz(max) = 60 mA.
outline: Worst case for Iz(min): Vin minimum 10 V with full load 50 mA
Check Iz at Vin = 14 V and no load: Iz = (14 − 6)/68 ≈ 118 mA, which exceeds Iz(max) — so the value must be revised or a larger Iz(max) part chosen
Zener power = Vz × Iz(max) = 6 × Iz(max)
Comment on why the two conditions pull Rs in opposite directions

bank.q: An NPN transistor with β = 100 has VCC = 12 V, RC = 1 kΩ and RB = 220 kΩ connected to VCC. Find IB, IC and VCE, and state the region of operation.
outline: IC = βIB ≈ 5.1 mA
VCE = VCC − IC × RC = 12 − 5.1 = 6.9 V
Since VCE is well above 0.2 V and the base junction is forward biased, the device is in the active region
Note what would change if RB were halved

bank.q: Design an op-amp circuit whose output is Vo = −(V1 + 2V2) using one op-amp and resistors, and another whose output is Vo = 3V1 − 2V2. Give resistor values and the input resistance seen by each source.
outline: Adder: inverting configuration with Rf = 10 kΩ, R1 = 10 kΩ for weight 1, R2 = 5 kΩ for weight 2
Vo = −Rf(V1/R1 + V2/R2); virtual ground at the inverting input makes the two inputs independent (summing point)
Subtractor: build the 3V1 − 2V2 from a difference amplifier, or from an inverter plus an adder
State that each source drives a resistance equal to its own input resistor
Mention that resistor ratios, not absolute values, set the gain

bank.q: Design a 555 astable circuit that produces a 1 kHz square wave with a duty cycle close to 50 percent, and a monostable circuit that gives a 2 ms pulse. Give component values and the formulas used.
outline: Astable: T = 0.693(RA + 2RB)C, duty cycle = (RA + RB)/(RA + 2RB)
Duty cycle near 50 percent needs RA much smaller than RB
Pick C = 10 nF and solve for RA and RB; state a practical standard value pair
Monostable: T = 1.1 RC, so for 2 ms with C = 1 μF, R ≈ 1.8 kΩ
Both timing levels come from the 1/3 and 2/3 VCC thresholds

bank.q: Derive the closed-loop gain of an inverting amplifier from the two golden rules, then analyse what happens when the open-loop gain is finite and when the frequency is high.
outline: Apply virtual ground and zero input current to write the node equation at the inverting input
Vo/Vi = −Rf/Rin, set purely by resistor ratio
With finite A, gain becomes −(Rf/Rin)/(1 + (1 + Rf/Rin)/A), so the error falls as A rises
At high frequency A falls at 20 dB per decade, so closed-loop gain is flat only up to the gain-bandwidth limit
Slew rate limits large-signal output slope; mention the virtual ground fails once the output saturates

bank.q: A 5 V relay coil drawing 80 mA must be switched from a 3.3 V microcontroller pin that can source only 5 mA. Compare a BJT switch and a MOSFET switch for this job and recommend one, giving the circuit.
outline: BJT: base resistor sized for IB = IC/β, at least 0.8 mA for β = 100; VBE = 0.7 V and the pin must supply base current continuously
MOSFET: gate draws only leakage current, so the pin drives it directly through a small series resistor
Add a freewheeling diode across the coil to absorb the inductive kick in both cases
BJT drops about 0.2 V in saturation; MOSFET drop set by RDS(on) × ID
Recommendation with justification and a note on the 3.3 V gate drive versus a logic-level MOSFET threshold

bank.q: Compare a Zener shunt regulator with a 78xx series regulator and with an LM317 for a 5 V, 500 mA supply, using load regulation, ripple rejection, dropout and protection as the criteria.
outline: Zener: simple and cheap, but load current must pass through Rs and Iz varies with load, so regulation is poor and efficiency low at high current
78xx: series pass transistor with feedback, internal current limit and thermal shutdown, ripple rejection typically around 60 dB, needs about 2 V dropout
LM317: adjustable from 1.25 V upward by a resistor divider, same protection features, dropout around 2 V at moderate current
500 mA is beyond comfortable Zener shunt design, so choose an IC regulator
Add input and output capacitors and note the heat dissipation of (Vin − 5 V) × 0.5 A

glossary.def: Pure silicon with no added impurity, in which the number of free electrons equals the number of holes and conductivity is very low.
The vacancy left when an electron leaves a covalent bond; it behaves as a positive charge carrier.
A pentavalent atom such as phosphorus or arsenic that donates a free electron and makes the silicon n-type.
A trivalent atom such as boron that creates a hole and makes the silicon p-type.
The boundary formed when p-type and n-type silicon are joined in one crystal, with a depletion region across it.
Connecting the p side to the positive terminal and the n side to the negative terminal, which narrows the depletion region and allows current above the knee voltage.
Connecting the p side to the negative terminal, which widens the depletion region and blocks current except for a small leakage.
Reverse breakdown in a lightly doped junction where carriers gain enough energy to knock out more carriers, creating a chain multiplication.
A circuit of diodes that converts alternating voltage into a one-directional (pulsating d.c.) voltage.
A diode circuit that removes the part of a waveform above or below a chosen level without changing the rest.
The d.c. values of collector current and collector-emitter voltage about which a transistor amplifier swings.
The BJT state where the base-emitter junction is not forward biased, so collector current is almost zero and the device acts as an open switch.
The BJT state where both junctions are forward biased, VCE falls to about 0.2 V and the device acts as a closed switch.
The conducting path between source and drain whose width is controlled by the gate voltage.
A FET type that conducts at zero gate-source voltage and is turned off by driving the gate voltage towards pinch-off.
A MOSFET type that is off at zero gate-source voltage and needs VGS above the threshold to form a channel.
The very large voltage gain (typically 10⁵ or about 100 dB) of an op-amp with no feedback.
Feeding a fraction of the output back to the inverting input so that the closed-loop gain is set by external components and becomes stable and predictable.
Common-mode rejection ratio, the ratio of differential gain to common-mode gain; ideally infinite, practically about 90 dB for a 741.
The small differential voltage (a few millivolts) needed at the inputs to make the output exactly zero, caused by imperfect matching inside the op-amp.
The change in output voltage when load current changes from no load to full load, usually given as a percentage or in millivolts.
The fraction of one period for which a pulse output stays high, expressed as a percentage.
